X.notes: Tests: npm test passed 8/8 in a temp copy. It matches the spec on every example and on the slugify and truncate probes: NFKD ligatures and Roman numerals, pre-decomposed marks, empty strings, max=1, all-whitespace prefix, NBSP, max=1.0, BigInt, '5', Symbol. Strengths: clean structure with named regex constants and an assertString helper (src/text.mjs:1-10), and an ELLIPSIS escape. It is the only suite that tells NFKD apart from NFD: slugify('ﬁle Ⅻ') === 'file-xii' (test/text.test.mjs:10). Invalid-max and non-string loops are reasonable (test:19, 39). That breaks the spec's RangeError contract. truncate('hello', Object.create(null)) throws TypeError 'Cannot convert object to primitive value', and a max whose toString throws passes that arbitrary Error through, where both should be RangeError. It also echoes caller input into error messages, and the message for BigInt 5n reads 'got 5'. reasoning: The three implementations are almost the same algorithm: lowercase, NFKD, drop U+0300-U+036F, collapse non-[a-z0-9] runs, trim dashes; for truncate, Number.isInteger plus slice/trimEnd/ellipsis. All three suites pass and all match the spec examples. They also share the same harmless quirks from following the spec order and the spec's .length semantics: '㎒' becomes 'z', and a surrogate pair can be split. They differ in three places. (1) X interpolates String(max) into its RangeError message. For a null-prototype or throwing-toString max, that throws TypeError or an arbitrary Error instead of the required RangeError. It is a real, if contrived, spec violation caused by extra code. Y and Z use static messages and are correct on every probe. (2) Code quality: Y is the cleanest, with a shared helper and readable \\u escapes. X is equally well structured apart from the interpolation. Z hides the key regex range in invisible literal combining characters and repeats the type check. (3) Tests: Y has the widest truncate boundary and type coverage. X alone checks NFKD over NFD. Z is the thinnest. Y is correct, clean and well tested, so it ranks first. Z is fully correct but harder to maintain and more thinly tested, so it beats X, whose only spec-compliance defect outweighs its slightly better structure and its unique NFKD test. None of the three has a real README.

X.notes: Strengths: the slugify/truncate pipeline is the same as the other two and gives the right result for every spec example and for every probe I ran (ligature/roman numeral via NFKD, pre-decomposed 'é', dotted I, emoji, CJK, String objects, Symbols, BigInt/'3'/undefined/NaN/Infinity max, empty input, whitespace-only prefix). String() itself can throw, so truncate('hello', Object.create(null)) throws 'TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value' instead of the RangeError the spec requires (reproduced). An object with a throwing toString would leak an arbitrary error the same way. reasoning: All three use the same algorithm (toLowerCase, then NFKD, then strip U+0300–U+036F, then collapse non-[a-z0-9] runs, then trim dashes; and slice(0, max-1).trimEnd() + '…'). All of them pass every spec example and their own tests (Z 9/9, Y 7/7, X 8/8) on Node 26, so the differences are at the margins. X.notes: Strengths: src/text.mjs (26 lines) follows the spec's steps in the order listed (toLowerCase, NFKD, strip U+0300-U+036F written as \u escapes on line 14, collapse [^a-z0-9]+, trim dashes). One shared assertString (lines 3-7). truncate (19-26) validates with Number.isInteger plus max<1, returns early when length<=max, and builds slice(0,max-1).trimEnd()+'…'. Every spec example passes, and so did my probes: '' -> '', max=1 -> '…', length==max returns the input, whitespace-only prefix -> '…', exotic max values (null-proto object, throwing toString, Symbol, BigInt, '5') all give RangeError, String objects give TypeError. npm test: 8/8 pass. The tests cover all spec examples, digits, leading and trailing dashes ('-Top 10 Items-'), empty input, length==max, max=1, an invalid-max list [0,-1,1.5,NaN,Infinity,'5',undefined], and non-string lists for both functions. Defects: (1) Because it lowercases before NFKD, compatibility characters that decompose to uppercase lose their letters: slugify('ℌello') and slugify('𝐇𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐨') give 'ello', '℡ 123' gives '123', and 'ᴬ' gives ''. That is 519 single code points in BMP+SMP1. It follows the literal step order, but the result is not fully 'lowercased text'. (2) The tests never check a cut in the middle of a word without whitespace beyond the spec example, and have no Unicode/NFKD case beyond Crème Brûlée. (3) The error message 'input must be a string' does not name the received type. (4) README.md is a one-line stub ('# bench project') with no usage or API docs.

Y.notes: In behaviour it is the same as X. My brute-force slugify comparison over U+0000-U+1FFFF found 0 differences, and truncate matches X on every probe except the error message text. That means it shares X's compatibility-character issue: 'ℌello' -> 'ello', '𝐇𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐨' -> 'ello', '℡ 123' -> '123'. Error path is solid: exotic max values all give RangeError, and the TypeError message names the type (src/text.mjs:5). npm test: 5/5 pass. Defects: (1) src/text.mjs:14 writes the combining-mark range as raw invisible characters, /[̀-ͯ]/g (bytes CC 80 - CD AF). It works, but it is unreadable, renders as stray diacritics on the brackets, and a re-encoding or editor normalization can corrupt it. The ̀-ͯ escape form used by X and Z is clearly better. Line 1 also uses a literal '…' rather than an escape. (2) Tests are coarse: only 5 test() blocks, each bundling many assertions, so the first failure hides the rest. 'slugify: spec examples' and 'truncate: spec examples' contain non-spec cases ('ABC 123', '', truncate('',1), max=1), so the names mislead. The truncate non-string test checks only 123 and null (lines 35-38). Coverage is still reasonable: length==max, max=1, empty input, and the invalid-max list. (3) README.md is a one-line stub.

Z.notes: Strengths: src/text.mjs names its regexes as module constants (COMBINING_MARKS, NON_ALPHANUMERIC_RUN, EDGE_DASHES, ELLIPSIS, lines 1-4) with \u escapes. Shared /g regexes are safe here because String.replace resets lastIndex. It runs NFKD before toLowerCase (lines 15-16), so the output is always fully lowercase and letters produced by decomposition survive: 'ℌello' -> 'hello', '𝐇𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐨' -> 'hello', '℡ 123' -> 'tel-123', 'ᴬ' -> 'a'. On 519 code points it beats X/Y, and it never gives a shorter result than they do. All spec examples and the plain edge cases match X/Y. npm test: 13/13 pass. Tests are the best of the three: one behaviour per test with descriptive names, an extra mid-word cut ('hello wor…'), length==max (11), max=1, full invalid-max and non-string lists for both functions, and NFKD compatibility tests (test/text.test.mjs:62-65) that pin the ordering choice. Defects: (1) src/text.mjs:25 builds the RangeError message with String(max), and that call can throw first. truncate('hello', Object.create(null)) throws TypeError 'Cannot convert object to primitive value', and a max with a throwing toString throws that arbitrary Error. Both break 'max must be an integer >= 1, otherwise throw a RangeError'; the inputs are exotic, but the bug comes from an embellishment of the error message. It also echoes caller values into error text. (2) It reorders the listed steps (NFKD before lowercase) with no comment explaining why; the result is better, but it is a silent deviation from the literal step order. (3) README.md is a one-line stub.

reasoning: All three pass their own tests, and the spec examples and ordinary edge cases give the same results in all three. Z ranks first because its tests are the most thorough and granular (13 focused tests, including the NFKD compatibility cases and a mid-word cut). Its normalize-then-lowercase order also keeps letters that X and Y turn into dashes (e.g. '𝐇𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐨' -> 'hello' vs 'ello'), and its named regex constants read best. It loses a point on robustness: building the error message with String(max) at src/text.mjs:25 makes truncate throw TypeError or an arbitrary Error, not RangeError, for a null-prototype or throwing-toString max. Those inputs are exotic, so the bug does not outweigh its advantages. X is clean, follows the steps literally, and its error paths are fully robust. Its tests are good but less thorough, and it shares the compatibility-letter loss. Y behaves identically to X: my brute-force comparison over U+0000-U+1FFFF found no slugify differences. It ranks last for two reasons: it writes the combining-mark range as invisible raw characters (src/text.mjs:14), which hurts readability and maintainability, and its tests are coarser, with fewer non-string cases and 'spec examples' blocks that mix in non-spec assertions. All three ship only a one-line README stub, so docs score the same.

X.notes: Strengths: src/text.mjs is minimal and clean. The steps follow the spec order (toLowerCase, then NFKD, then strip U+0300-U+036F with readable \u escapes at :14, collapse non-[a-z0-9] runs, trim dashes). Number.isInteger plus max<1 gives RangeError for 0, -1, 1.5, NaN, Infinity, '5', undefined, 5n and Symbol. Its static error message means exotic max values (null-prototype object, object whose toString throws) still get RangeError. It throws TypeError for non-strings, including new String('x'). Every spec example passes, and so did these probes: equal-length boundary, max=1 gives '…', '' gives '', multiple trailing spaces trimmed, NBSP trimmed. All 8 tests pass. Defects: because it lowercases before NFKD (the literal spec order), about 500 compatibility capitals are dropped instead of kept as lowercase letters: 'ℌello' gives 'ello', '𝐀BC' gives 'bc', '㋎x' gives 'e-x'. That is defensible under a literal reading but leaves non-lowercase letters to be stripped. The TypeError message 'input must be a string' (:5) gives no detail. The tests (test/text.test.mjs) cover the spec examples, the boundary at :29-31, max=1, invalid max and non-string, but nothing tells NFKD apart from NFD (an NFD implementation would pass every test), and truncate('') is not tested. README.md is only the placeholder '# bench project', with no usage or API docs.

Y.notes: Strengths: the logic is the same as X's and correct to the letter of the spec (lowercase, NFKD, strip marks, collapse runs, trim). RangeError and TypeError validation is correct for every probe, including null-prototype objects, BigInt and Symbol, and the 'got <typeof>' TypeError message is useful. Every spec example passes, and so did the boundary probes: equal length, max=1, '' with max=1, trailing whitespace trimmed. All 5 tests pass. Defects: src/text.mjs:14 writes the combining-mark range as raw invisible characters (/[̀-ͯ]/g; bytes CC 80 to CD AF). It works, but a reader cannot see it, and an editor that normalizes text could silently break it. The ellipsis at :1 is also a raw character rather than …. Like X, it drops compatibility capitals ('ℌello' gives 'ello'). Tests: only 5 coarse test() blocks, each packing many asserts ('spec examples' at :5-12 and :20-27), so one failure hides the rest. truncate's TypeError is checked for just 123 and null (:35-38). Z.notes: Strengths: src/text.mjs names its regexes and the ellipsis as constants (:1-4) and uses one assertString helper. It runs NFKD before toLowerCase (:15-16), so the slug really is lowercase even for compatibility capitals: 'ℌello' gives 'hello', '𝐀BC' gives 'abc'. I brute-forced every code point: Z keeps a letter in 499 cases where X and Y drop it, and never the reverse. The steps are in a different order from the spec's list, but the output better meets 'Lowercase the text'. Every spec example passes, and so did the boundary probes (equal length, max=1, '', trailing spaces and NBSP). Error messages are informative. Tests: 13 focused cases, all passing. It is the only solution whose tests check NFKD rather than NFD ('ﬁle' gives 'file', 'ℌello' gives 'hello' at test/text.test.mjs:62-65). Tests also cover digits, an extra truncate length (10), max=1 and a wide set of invalid max values. Defects: the RangeError message at :25 calls String(max). For a null-prototype object it therefore throws TypeError ('Cannot convert object to primitive value'), and for an object whose toString throws it rethrows that object's own error, instead of the RangeError the spec requires ('otherwise throw a RangeError'). These inputs are contrived, but the cosmetic message breaks the error contract, and no test covers it. Its compute order differs from the spec's listed order, which a strict literal reading could mark against it. README.md is a placeholder.

reasoning:
All three are very close. All pass every spec example and their own tests (Z 13/13, X 8/8, Y 5/5). All validate types and integers correctly for ordinary inputs. All three READMEs are placeholders.

Z ranks first. It has the best tests: it is the only suite that checks the spec's NFKD requirement, which an NFD implementation would fail, and its cases are the most granular. Its code is the clearest, with named constants. Running NFKD before lowercasing gives a correct lowercase slug for compatibility characters that X and Y silently drop; a brute force over all code points showed Z keeps the letter in 499 cases and never loses one. Against that, its String(max) error message breaks the RangeError contract for exotic max values. That is a real but contrived defect, and it costs robustness points.

X ranks second. It is clean, follows the spec order literally, uses readable \u escapes, and always throws the right error type. Its tests are adequate but would not notice NFD in place of NFKD.

Y ranks last. Its logic is the same as X's, but its source has invisible raw combining characters in the regex, a real readability and maintenance hazard. Its tests are the thinnest: 5 coarse blocks with sparse truncate TypeError cases.

X.notes: Strengths: all 71 of its own tests pass. Every spec line I probed behaves correctly: join/trim, Usage on stderr with exit 2 (also for prototype keys and an empty command, todo.mjs:116), invalid id vs not found, idempotent done, ids never reused after remove or clear-done, and corrupt-file exit 3 with the file left byte-identical. Input is validated before the load (todo.mjs:76-78, 92-93), so `add` with empty text on a corrupt file still says 'text required'. Shape validation covers each todo item (todo.mjs:28-35); null, arrays, `[5]` and items with no text are all rejected as corrupt. Exit codes are named constants (todo.mjs:15-17), updates are immutable, the temp file name uses pid and a timestamp in the same folder (todo.mjs:51), and process.exitCode lets output flush. Tests (test/todo.test.mjs) are the strongest of the three. They use exact {code, stdout, stderr} deepEqual, 7 invalid-id variants per command with a file-unchanged check (156-173), not-found on a missing file without creating it, 0 and -1, 5 corrupt contents x 5 commands with no temp files left behind (233-253), default and empty TODO_FILE (61-70), non-ASCII text, and afterEach cleanup. Defects: (1) I/O errors other than CliError are rethrown (todo.mjs:124), so a directory as TODO_FILE or a missing parent folder prints a raw Node stack trace. (2) It does not check that lastId >= the highest id. A hand-edited {lastId:0, todos:[{id:1,...}]} lets `add` create a duplicate #1 (probed). (3) existsSync followed by readFileSync is a small TOCTOU gap (todo.mjs:38-39). (4) Huge ids like 99999999999999999999 print 'not found #100000000000000000000'; all three share this. (5) clear-done on a missing file creates the file; harmless. README is accurate and concise and includes an exit-code table.

Y.notes: Strengths: all 12 of its own tests pass. CLI behaviour on every spec line matched X exactly in my probes. It has the most robust load (todo.mjs:24-44). It validates every item and the invariant id < nextId, so a hand-edited file that would cause id reuse is reported as corrupt instead of creating duplicate ids. ENOENT is handled without a TOCTOU gap. Unexpected I/O errors become a friendly 'Error: <message>' with exit 1 (todo.mjs:121-122) and no stack trace. Input is validated before the load. The temp file sits in the same folder (todo.mjs:47), and the README documents exit 1 for I/O errors. Defects: (1) Tests are thin: 12 coarse tests. Many setup steps are not asserted (run('add','a') with no check, test/todo.test.mjs:217-219, 230-235). The whitespace-add case checks only the exit code (211). Bad-shape cases run only `list` (278-284). There is no test for a file stored out of order, for 0/-1 ids, or for a missing file on done/remove. Test temp dirs are never cleaned up (no afterEach rmSync). (2) Exit codes are magic numbers scattered in the code (todo.mjs:36,41,58,64,71,111,122). isTodo is a closure inside load that captures data (todo.mjs:38-39). (3) The I/O error message includes the absolute path. That is acceptable for a local CLI. (4) The README says code 3 means 'not valid JSON' but omits that a bad shape also counts as corrupt. (5) It shares the huge-id echo quirk. The unused-looking 'bin' entry in package.json is harmless.

Z.notes: Strengths: all 25 of its own tests pass. The architecture is the cleanest: commands are pure (data, args) -> {data, out} and main alone loads and saves (todo.mjs:68-113), with the 'Error: ' prefix added in one place. On well-formed data, every spec behaviour I probed matched X and Y. Tests are good. They use t.after cleanup, exact deepEqual, an asserted `ok` helper for setup steps, out-of-order file sorting, id reuse after remove and after clear-done, 0/-1/leading zeros, 4 corrupt contents x 5 commands with a byte-for-byte unchanged check, the default todo.json and no leftover temp files. The README is the most complete: a section per command with examples, the id parsing rules, the exact usage text, the data-file shape and an exit-code table. Defects: (1) Shape validation is top-level only (todo.mjs:23-26) and never checks todo items. With {lastId:1, todos:[null]}, `list` and `done 1` crash with a TypeError stack trace and exit 1. `todos:[5]` makes list print '#undefined [ ] undefined'. A todo with no text lists as 'undefined'. In all of these cases `add` and `done` happily rewrite the malformed file (probed). (2) Like X, it does not check lastId >= max id, so a hand-edited file gives duplicate ids. (3) I/O errors (EISDIR, missing parent folder) are rethrown as raw stack traces (todo.mjs:109). (4) It loads before validating arguments (todo.mjs:104), so `add` with no text or `done abc` on a corrupt file reports corrupt (exit 3) instead of the usage error. The spec does not fix the order, so this is defensible, but it is inconsistent with the parse-first reading. (5) Tests never cover malformed todo items, which is exactly where the code fails. It shares the huge-id echo quirk.

reasoning: All three solutions pass their own tests and behave identically on every spec-defined input I probed. That covers join/trim, empty text, list formatting and sorting, idempotent done, invalid id vs not found (including '', 1.5, +1, 0x1, 0, -1 and 01), clear-done counts, Usage for no, unknown and prototype-key commands, and exit 3 on corrupt JSON with the file untouched. They differ in robustness and test depth. X ranks first: it is correct and cleanly structured, and its test suite is clearly the best (71 exact-equality tests, including file-unchanged checks across 5 corrupt contents x 5 commands). Its weaknesses are environmental I/O errors surfacing as stack traces and no lastId invariant check. Y has the most robust implementation: full item validation, an id < nextId invariant and friendly I/O errors. Its tests are much thinner (12 coarse tests, unasserted setup steps, leaked temp dirs), so it sits just behind X. Z has the nicest architecture and the best README. However, its load validates only top-level shape, so malformed todo items crash list and done with a TypeError, print 'undefined' entries, and get rewritten by add. Z also prints raw stack traces on I/O errors, and its tests miss exactly that gap, which puts it last.
